Renaming the field immediately or relying on mocks alone does not protect the still-running old support service.
micro.explanation: Expand-then-contract evolution creates a compatibility interval across independently deployed components; the removal step still requires evidence and ownership.
criteria: Choose additive compatible evolution.
Include evidence before removal.
Recognize independent deployment needs contract discipline.
options: Rename the field immediately because services hide implementation details.
Keep both fields temporarily, test compatibility and retire the old one after migration.
Require both services to deploy in one atomic release forever.
Change only the mock service because production clients will adapt automatically.

micro.title: Parallel calls do not remove every dependency
micro.question: A dashboard endpoint first checks access in 20 ms, then fetches warehouse inventory in 90 ms and carrier status in 140 ms. The last two reads are independent and can run concurrently. Rendering takes 15 ms after both return. Ignore network variability and queueing. Calculate sequential and parallel response times, then propose behavior when the carrier call takes two seconds but warehouse data remains useful.
micro.hint: Parallel branches contribute their maximum duration; the access check still comes first.
micro.answer: Sequential execution takes 20 + 90 + 140 + 15 = 265 ms. Running the independent reads together takes 20 + max(90, 140) + 15 = 175 ms, a 90 ms reduction under the stated assumptions. Parallelism does not remove the slowest dependency. Set a carrier deadline consistent with the page budget and return clearly marked partial or cached carrier information only if product requirements permit it. Preserve the access check before exposing either dataset. Bound outstanding calls and retries so a slow carrier does not accumulate unbounded work across dashboard requests.
micro.explanation: This calculation concerns a dependency graph, not a throughput guarantee. Timeout and partial-result policies determine how the architecture behaves beyond the ideal timing case.
criteria: Compute 265 ms and 175 ms correctly.
State partial-result/deadline semantics.
Bound dependency work while retaining authorization.

micro.title: Independent code, shared schema
micro.question: An insurance company labels claims and reporting as separate microservices. Both have write access to the same claim tables, and reporting updates a processed flag that claims uses to decide whether a record may be edited. A reporting schema migration now blocks claims releases. Identify the coupling and propose a staged boundary repair that keeps reporting available during migration.
micro.hint: Look for shared ownership of business state, not just separate repositories.
micro.answer: The services share schema and business-invariant ownership, so separate processes have not produced independent change boundaries. Assign claim lifecycle state to one authoritative owner and expose a supported API or event contract for reporting. Give reporting a derived read model whose processing progress does not directly control claim edits. During migration, populate and validate the read model alongside the existing path, define acceptable lag and reconciliation, then remove reporting’s direct writes. Avoid an immediate database split without preserving semantics. If reporting truly controls an edit constraint, model that interaction explicitly instead of hiding it in a shared flag.
micro.explanation: A boundary is defined by ownership and contracts as well as deployment. A derived reporting model can reduce coupling but introduces freshness and reconciliation obligations.
criteria: Identify schema and invariant ownership coupling.
Propose explicit authority and contract.
Stage migration with reconciliation and lag semantics.

load-balancing.title: Connection count hides the work
load-balancing.question: A reverse proxy selects the backend with the fewest open connections. Backend A has one HTTP/2 connection carrying 80 active requests, while backend B has ten connections carrying one active request each. All requests require similar CPU time and the machines have equal capacity. The proxy repeatedly sends new work to A. Which observation most directly explains why the policy is making a poor choice?
load-balancing.hint: The metric counts transport connections, not necessarily concurrent application work.
load-balancing.answer: Connection count is a poor load proxy when one connection multiplexes many requests. A has fewer connections but more active application work in this scenario. Consider an implementation that accounts for active requests, measured outstanding work or another suitable load signal, and verify behavior with the actual protocol configuration. Simply reversing least-connections into most-connections would also be brittle: connection lifetimes, idle connections and request cost can change. CPU and queue metrics may help, but each has reporting delay and overhead. The correct policy follows the workload rather than a universal ranking of algorithms.
load-balancing.explanation: HTTP/2 breaks an assumed one-connection-to-one-request relationship. Equal hardware does not rescue a metric that measures the wrong unit of work.
criteria: Recognize multiplexing mismatch.
Choose a workload-relevant metric.
Avoid claiming one routing algorithm is universally best.
options: DNS always sends clients to the wrong continent.
A has less work because it has fewer connections.
One connection can carry many requests, so connection count understates A’s load.
B must be unhealthy because it has more connections.

load-balancing.title: Capacity while draining
load-balancing.question: A video-metadata service has six identical stateless workers. Each sustains 180 requests per second while meeting the latency target. Peak incoming traffic is 780 requests per second. Operations want to drain two workers simultaneously for an upgrade and retain 20% capacity headroom on the remaining workers. Using a simple additive-capacity model, determine whether this plan meets the target and how many workers must remain active.
load-balancing.hint: Twenty percent headroom means offered load uses at most 80% of available target-compliant capacity.
load-balancing.answer: Four remaining workers provide 4 × 180 = 720 requests per second, already below the 780 arrival rate. With 20% headroom, the usable budget is only 0.8 × 720 = 576. The requirement is n × 180 × 0.8 ≥ 780, so n ≥ 5.417 and at least six workers must remain active. Under this model, the current fleet cannot drain even one worker while preserving that headroom. Add temporary capacity, reduce admitted traffic or schedule the change below peak. Confirm the shared database and balancer can support the plan; additive worker capacity is an assumption, not a measurement.
load-balancing.explanation: Headroom is a constraint on capacity during maintenance, not merely on the normal fleet. Draining also needs a policy for in-flight requests and a deadline.
criteria: Calculate four-worker deficit and 576 budget.
Derive at least six active workers.
State a feasible maintenance adjustment and model limitations.

load-balancing.title: Diagnosing a faraway edge
load-balancing.question: Customers in Oslo sometimes reach a CDN edge in London rather than an available Stockholm edge. The hostname may use DNS steering, and some published addresses are anycast. Support concludes that the CDN is broken because Stockholm is geographically closer. Propose measurements that distinguish resolver-based steering, route selection and cache/origin latency before deciding whether the service is actually worse.
load-balancing.hint: Geography, routing policy and measured application latency are different quantities.
load-balancing.answer: Compare DNS answers and TTLs from affected clients and their actual recursive resolvers, noting whether steering has client-network information. Identify the selected edge using provider diagnostics, and measure connection and application timings over repeated samples rather than assuming physical proximity predicts latency. For anycast addresses, inspect routing observations where available, while recognizing a path trace alone is not a complete performance explanation. Separate fresh cache hits from misses or revalidations that contact the origin. Compare latency, errors and load at both candidate paths. A London edge may perform better because of peering, capacity or policy even when it is farther away.
load-balancing.explanation: DNS chooses an address under a policy; anycast routing selects a path to an advertisement; the response may then require an origin fetch. Each stage can explain latency.
criteria: Measure resolver/answer and edge selection separately.
Distinguish anycast policy from distance.
Separate hit/miss origin effects and compare observed outcomes.

push.title: A shared tablet changes users
push.question: A clinic tablet receives appointment push messages through one installed app. Patient A signs out and patient B signs in on the same installation. The push provider has not changed the installation token. A delayed message for A is still queued. Which design best limits accidental disclosure while allowing the installation to receive future notifications for B?
push.hint: An installation destination and the currently authorized account are not identical.
push.answer: Update the authenticated account-to-installation binding on logout and login, and keep sensitive content out of an unauthenticated notification preview. Send a minimal notification that prompts the app to fetch authorized account data; the app must reject or ignore account-mismatched stale messages. Removing A’s backend binding prevents future routing but cannot necessarily recall a provider-queued message. Token rotation alone is not a complete confidentiality mechanism. The design should also clear local account data and define whether any notifications may appear while signed out. Delivery to the same installation does not confer permission to show one patient’s details to another.
push.explanation: The privacy boundary is the account session, while the provider routes to an installation. A queued message can outlive the account-to-device association that caused it.
criteria: Distinguish installation from account.
Handle already queued stale messages.
Require authorized fetch or account-safe presentation.
options: Keep A’s binding because a provider token permanently identifies a person.
Put full appointment details in every push so the app need not check identity.
Assume logout automatically deletes all messages queued by the provider.
Refresh account bindings and use minimal notifications followed by authorized account-scoped fetches.

push.title: Comparing connection overhead
push.question: A foreground monitoring app has 2,400 active devices. Design P polls every 15 seconds, including when nothing changes. Design S uses one established stream per device and sends a keepalive every 45 seconds. Ignoring setup, retries and actual event traffic, estimate messages per minute for each design, counting one poll exchange as two messages and one keepalive as one message. Explain why these counts alone do not prove a battery-life advantage.
push.hint: Count per-device traffic first, then multiply; a keepalive is not the complete energy model.
push.answer: Design P performs four poll exchanges per device per minute, or eight messages: 2,400 × 8 = 19,200 messages per minute. Design S averages 60/45 keepalives per device per minute, giving 3,200 messages per minute. That is one sixth of the counted messages under the stated convention. Energy also depends on payload sizes, radio wakeups and tail time, batching, connection maintenance, network loss, TLS setup and operating-system scheduling. Measure the real device workload before claiming battery savings. The stream also needs reconnect, resynchronization and server connection capacity; fewer messages do not establish reliable event delivery.
push.explanation: The arithmetic isolates idle protocol overhead. It deliberately excludes the physical and operating-system costs that make message count an incomplete energy proxy.
criteria: Compute 19,200 and 3,200 messages/minute.
Respect the counting assumptions.
Explain energy and delivery limitations.

push.title: An old disconnect deletes a new connection
push.question: A notification router stores user U → worker A, connection 7. U reconnects through worker B, which replaces the record with connection 8. A delayed disconnect callback from A then deletes the record by user ID alone. Later alerts cannot find U even though connection 8 is healthy. Design registration and cleanup semantics that handle this race and explain how the same scheme can support two legitimate devices.
push.hint: Cleanup should prove ownership of the registration it removes.
push.answer: Store a connection identifier or generation with the owner, and delete only if the stored entry still matches the disconnecting connection. A’s callback for connection 7 then cannot remove connection 8. Use atomic compare-and-delete or equivalent versioned storage semantics, and consider expiring leases for owners that disappear without callbacks. For multiple devices, key registrations by authenticated account plus installation or connection identity, yielding a set of valid destinations rather than one user-wide slot. Authorize registration changes and bound stale entries. Reconnection should also trigger state reconciliation, since a correct directory does not recover events missed during the gap.
push.explanation: The race is stale ownership, not merely network failure. Versioned cleanup preserves the newest registration without preventing intentionally concurrent destinations.
criteria: Use generation/connection-scoped atomic cleanup.
Support a destination set per user.
Address stale leases and missed-event recovery.

security.title: Recovery must not bypass the guard
security.question: A document-sharing service loses connectivity to its authorization database. Engineers suggest temporarily allowing any authenticated account to download a document if it knows the document ID, arguing that IDs are difficult to guess and this preserves availability. The documents include confidential contracts. Which response best follows fail-safe defaults without confusing authentication with authorization?
security.hint: Knowing an identifier is not evidence of an access grant.
security.answer: Deny protected downloads when permission cannot be established, while returning an appropriate temporary-failure response and allowing genuinely public operations to continue. Authentication establishes an account context, not permission for every document, and hard-to-guess identifiers are not a replacement for the intended authorization policy. A previously established bounded authorization cache could be considered only if its freshness and revocation risk were explicitly accepted in advance. The outage should trigger operational recovery, not an improvised expansion of privileges. Availability matters, but this proposed fallback changes the confidentiality policy precisely when the guard cannot evaluate it.
security.explanation: Fail-safe defaults require an explicit grant, not a guess that a requester probably has one. A degraded mode must be designed against the actual security policy.
criteria: Choose fail-closed protected access.
Separate public availability from confidential authorization.
Reject secret-looking IDs as substitute permissions.
options: Deny protected downloads without established permission and preserve permitted public operations.
Allow access only for long document IDs.
Allow downloads because authentication proves all necessary permission.
Log every unauthorized download and approve it automatically.

security.title: A one-use export ticket
security.question: A research archive wants to issue a download ticket for one restricted dataset. The ticket should work for ten minutes and permit only one completed export. Workers are stateless, and the ticket is signed by the archive. Two requests carrying the same valid ticket arrive at different workers simultaneously. Explain why signing and expiry are insufficient and design the shared decision needed to enforce the one-use requirement.
security.hint: Integrity, lifetime and consumption count are separate properties.
security.answer: The signature protects ticket integrity and the expiry limits its time window, but both concurrent requests can satisfy those checks. Give the ticket a unique identifier, bind it to the intended dataset and operation, and atomically claim or consume it in authoritative shared storage. Define what counts as completed export and how an interrupted transfer resumes without creating a second authorization; a short-lived claimed state or a stable export job can separate retries from new consumption. Enforce account binding if the policy requires it. Document whether revocation is checked before use and how failure between claiming and delivery is recovered.
security.explanation: A stateless verifier can validate a signature but cannot independently know whether another worker consumed the same ticket. The one-use invariant needs coordinated state or an equivalent authority.
criteria: Distinguish authenticity/expiry from replay prevention.
Use atomic shared consumption and scope binding.
Define retry and interrupted-delivery semantics.

security.title: Diagnostics with bounded authority
security.question: A customer-support team needs enough diagnostic data to investigate failed file uploads. A proposed debug endpoint returns environment variables, request headers and the last 500 log lines, and runs under the same account that can delete stored files. Design a narrower diagnostic interface. Identify one confidentiality risk, one integrity risk and one availability risk, and specify useful information support can still obtain.
security.hint: Useful diagnostics do not require arbitrary secret or administrative access.
security.answer: Expose a bounded, structured report with correlation IDs, sanitized error categories, timestamps, upload sizes and relevant service status. Redact credentials and sensitive content from headers, logs and environment data to address confidentiality. Run report generation with read-only, scoped access rather than file-deletion authority, reducing integrity risk. Bound report size, query cost and request rate so repeated diagnostics cannot exhaust the service, addressing availability. Authorize access to the relevant customer or case, audit sensitive report requests and define retention. Keep deeper privileged investigation behind a separate controlled workflow instead of expanding every support session’s authority.
security.explanation: This design applies least privilege to both data disclosure and execution authority. Bounded work prevents a troubleshooting feature from becoming an uncontrolled resource consumer.
criteria: Identify concrete CIA risks.
Preserve useful sanitized diagnostics.
Limit authority and resource consumption.

styles.title: Interpreting a workflow language
styles.question: A laboratory application lets technicians save experiment recipes in a small language with variables, conditional branches and repeat-until steps. At runtime an execution engine reads the recipe, maintains variable values and chooses the next operation. Hardware adapters perform permitted instrument actions. Which architectural description best explains the recipe-execution core, without claiming that the entire application has only one style?
styles.hint: Ask which component assigns meaning to the saved program and maintains execution state.
styles.answer: The core follows an interpreter or virtual-machine style: the recipe is a program representation, the engine evaluates its constructs, and stored variables plus control position form execution state. Hardware adapters may separately use object-oriented or client-server patterns. Calling every sequence of steps a pipe-and-filter system would miss the branching and mutable execution context described here. A central recipe store alone also does not explain execution semantics. The style label is useful because it highlights language validation, resource limits and separation between user-defined programs and the trusted engine, while allowing a hybrid overall architecture.
styles.explanation: The defining relationship is an engine giving semantics to a program representation. Storage location and the existence of several steps are secondary features.
criteria: Identify interpreter/VM core.
Relate components to program and execution state.
Allow hybrid styles around the core.
options: Pure pipe and filter because the recipe has more than one step.
Interpreter/virtual-machine style because an engine evaluates a program representation.
Peer-to-peer because many technicians author recipes.
Repository style alone because recipes can be saved.

styles.title: A pipeline whose buffer keeps growing
styles.question: A document-processing pipeline has three filters: parsing at 120 documents per second, classification at 70, and indexing at 100. A producer supplies 90 documents per second continuously. Assume average rates are stable, no documents are discarded and parsing can keep up. Identify the bottleneck, estimate buffer growth before classification over two minutes, and propose controls that preserve correctness rather than hiding the overload.
styles.hint: Compare the arrival rate at each stage with that stage’s sustainable completion rate.
styles.answer: Classification is the bottleneck at 70 documents per second, so the upstream queue gains 90 − 70 = 20 documents per second, or 2,400 over two minutes under these assumptions. Indexing has capacity for the classifier’s output but cannot repair the earlier deficit. Use bounded buffers and backpressure, or durably admit work under an explicit backlog policy. Scaling classification is useful only if documents can be processed independently and ordering or shared-model constraints remain satisfied. Measure sustainable rates and provide lag observability. Silently dropping documents or adding an unlimited in-memory queue would violate the stated correctness requirement.
styles.explanation: Pipes decouple stages through an agreed record flow, but they do not create capacity. Buffering absorbs a finite burst; sustained excess arrival requires capacity or admission changes.
criteria: Find 70/s bottleneck and 2,400-document growth.
Propose bounded backpressure or durable admission.
Discuss parallelism and correctness constraints.

styles.title: Feedback with stale measurements
styles.question: A greenhouse controller samples humidity every second and opens a mist valve whenever the latest reading is below a target. A network change delays sensor messages by 25 seconds, yet the controller treats every arriving sample as current. Humidity now repeatedly overshoots the target. Explain the architectural failure and propose sensing, control and safety boundaries; you do not need to derive a numerical control law.
styles.hint: A feedback decision depends on when the measurement describes the plant, not merely when it arrives.
styles.answer: The controller is acting on delayed plant state, so it can keep adding moisture after the real humidity has crossed the target. Carry measurement timestamps, detect stale or out-of-order observations and make delay an explicit control-design assumption. Use an appropriate tested control strategy with bounded actuation rather than repeatedly reacting as if each sample were current. Define a safe stale-sensor behavior, maximum valve-open duration and independent limits where the hazard warrants them. Observe actuator status as well as sensor values. Separating sensing, decision logic and actuation clarifies responsibilities but does not itself guarantee stability.
styles.explanation: Process-control architecture makes the feedback loop central. Communication delay is part of that loop and must be considered alongside sensing accuracy and actuator behavior.
criteria: Explain delayed feedback and overshoot.
Track freshness and bound actuation.
Separate responsibilities without claiming automatic stability.

secure.title: Signing-key rotation without accepting strangers
secure.question: An identity provider rotates from signing key K1 to K2. A reporting service caches the provider’s trusted verification keys and has not refreshed them, so valid K2 tokens fail. An engineer suggests reading an arbitrary key URL from each token header and fetching that key whenever verification fails. Which response restores rotation support without allowing a token sender to choose its own trust authority?
secure.hint: Key discovery must remain anchored to configured trusted issuers.
secure.answer: Refresh keys only through the configured trusted issuer’s key-distribution mechanism, with controlled caching and bounded retry behavior. Allow planned overlap for K1 and K2 as the issuer’s policy requires, and verify issuer, audience, permitted algorithms and token lifetime in addition to the signature. Do not trust an arbitrary header-supplied URL as a new authority: a malicious sender could offer a key for its own signature or induce unwanted outbound requests. Unknown keys should fail closed if trusted refresh cannot resolve them. Rotation monitoring helps distinguish a rollout problem from malformed or hostile tokens.
secure.explanation: The token may identify a key within a trusted set, but it must not redefine who is trusted. Rotation changes key material while preserving the trust anchor.
criteria: Keep discovery anchored to trusted configuration.
Handle caching/overlap without bypassing validation.
Fail closed for unresolved untrusted keys.
options: Fetch any URL the token advertises and trust its result.
Disable signature checks until the next deployment.
Refresh through the configured trusted issuer and retain normal claim validation.
Accept unknown keys if the token has a plausible username.

secure.title: Measuring the revocation window
secure.question: An access token is issued at 14:00 and expires at 14:12. At 14:03 an operator revokes its refresh token after suspected theft. API workers verify access tokens locally and do not consult a revocation list. Assume synchronized clocks and no expiration grace. How much longer can the stolen access token be accepted, and what changes could shorten that window without pretending refresh-token revocation already solves it?
secure.hint: Issuance of future tokens and acceptance of an existing token are separate decisions.
secure.answer: The existing access token can remain acceptable until 14:12, leaving nine minutes after the 14:03 action, assuming its other checks pass. Revoking the refresh token prevents authorized renewal through that credential but does not update a self-contained token already held by an attacker. Shorter access-token lifetimes reduce the maximum window. Introspection, a revocation list or a subject/session version check can support earlier rejection, with explicit propagation and cache freshness guarantees. These add dependencies and operational cost, so define their outage behavior. Rotating a shared signing key can invalidate many unrelated sessions and is not a precise per-session remedy.
secure.explanation: The calculation exposes the tradeoff between offline verification and rapidly changing authority. A design must state revocation latency rather than simply claiming tokens are revocable.
criteria: Calculate nine minutes.
Separate refresh and access-token effects.
Offer explicit early-rejection mechanisms and tradeoffs.

secure.title: A useful URL-fetching feature
secure.question: A media service accepts a customer-supplied image URL and fetches it to create a thumbnail. It runs inside a cluster with access to private administration endpoints. Product requirements need only HTTPS images from two partner domains, but the current implementation follows every redirect and allows any hostname. Design validation and network boundaries for this feature, including what must be rechecked after a redirect.
secure.hint: A URL that looked acceptable before resolution or redirect may lead somewhere else.
secure.answer: Allow only the required scheme, partner hostnames and expected ports, using a real URL parser and a defined normalization policy. Resolve and restrict destinations so private administration or metadata addresses are not reachable, accounting for resolution changes. Either disallow redirects or revalidate every redirected URL and resolved destination under the same policy. Enforce outbound network restrictions as a separate boundary, and give the fetching workload minimal internal authority. Bound response size, time and decoding resources, then verify the content is an acceptable image. Log safe diagnostic metadata without secrets. An allowlist check on only the first URL is insufficient.
secure.explanation: The intended feature is a narrow outbound capability. Validation constrains logical destinations, while network and resource controls limit consequences if parsing or application logic fails.
criteria: Validate every destination including redirects/resolution.
Combine application policy with egress/least privilege.
Bound fetch and image-processing resources.

pushcase.title: Which queued update may replace another?
pushcase.question: A courier platform queues two types of messages for an offline driver: complete route-location snapshots and signed proof-of-delivery records for different parcels. Storage is under pressure. The latest snapshot contains all location state needed by the map, while every proof record is independently required for audit. Which compaction policy preserves the stated semantics without assuming every notification is replaceable?
pushcase.hint: Distinguish superseding state snapshots from independent business records.
pushcase.answer: Coalesce older route-location snapshots into the newest complete snapshot for the same scope, but preserve each distinct proof-of-delivery record in durable authoritative storage. A notification about a proof may be retried or regenerated from that record, rather than making the transient delivery queue its only copy. Define snapshot version and scope so unrelated routes are not collapsed together. Expiry can make an old location snapshot unhelpful, but it does not authorize deleting audit evidence. The policy follows business meaning: message arrival order or a shared destination alone does not establish that one payload supersedes another.
pushcase.explanation: Compaction is valid only when the retained information replaces everything the discarded message was required to convey. Business-event durability belongs beyond a best-effort push queue.
criteria: Coalesce only scoped superseding snapshots.
Preserve independent audit records durably.
Separate notification transport from authoritative evidence.
options: Keep every location snapshot but combine unrelated proof records into one arbitrary record.
Keep only the last message for the driver, regardless of type.
Discard all proofs because the provider accepted their notification requests.
Keep the newest scoped location snapshot and preserve each required proof record.

pushcase.title: A burst with an expiry budget
pushcase.question: A real-time delivery tier receives a burst of 18,000 independent advisory messages at time zero. It can transmit 600 messages per second at a constant rate, has no other traffic and serves FIFO. Every message expires 20 seconds after creation. In a fluid approximation, how many can be sent before expiry and how many become stale? Propose a response that distinguishes operational alerts from guaranteed business actions.
pushcase.hint: Calculate the work completed inside the freshness window, not the time needed to empty the queue.
pushcase.answer: The tier can transmit 600 × 20 = 12,000 messages within the window, leaving 6,000 stale messages in this approximation. Draining all 18,000 would take 30 seconds, so sending the remaining third later would violate the stated freshness policy. Discard or suppress expired advisories and record their outcome; prioritize only if the contract permits it. Add capacity or reduce admitted advisory work when the expected burst exceeds the freshness budget. If some messages represent essential business actions, persist those actions separately and expose authoritative status or recovery rather than treating an expired notification as cancellation of the action.
pushcase.explanation: A queue smooths a burst only within its capacity and freshness constraints. Delivery acceptance and durable business completion are different reliability boundaries.
criteria: Compute 12,000 sent, 6,000 stale and 30-second drain time.
Respect expiry rather than blindly drain.
Separate advisory freshness from business durability.

pushcase.title: Acknowledgement lost after application
pushcase.question: A warehouse handheld receives message M77 instructing it to display a task confirmation already committed in the backend. The device records M77 and updates its screen, but its acknowledgement is lost during a disconnect. The delivery tier replays M77 after reconnection. Design the device and server state needed for safe replay, and explain why provider acceptance, device receipt and a worker reading the confirmation are different milestones.
pushcase.hint: Retry the delivery without repeating an irreversible application effect.
pushcase.answer: Give messages stable IDs and define an acknowledgement as a specific processing milestone. The device records M77’s processed status durably enough for the promised replay window and applies any local effect idempotently, then acknowledges duplicates without repeating that effect. Coordinate local recording and application so a crash does not create an ambiguous half-completion, or rebuild the view from authoritative backend state. The server retains replay state until acknowledgement or its documented expiry and does not interpret provider acceptance as device processing. A displayed confirmation still does not prove a human saw or acted on it; that requires a separate explicit interaction.
pushcase.explanation: A lost acknowledgement makes duplicate delivery normal. End-to-end effects need deduplication or idempotency at the consumer, and each reported success must name its actual boundary.
criteria: Use stable IDs and consumer replay-safe effects.
Define retention/expiry and crash behavior.
Separate transport, device and human milestones.

jeromy-evaluation.title: Follow the full path
jeromy-evaluation.question: Reliability is ranked second among three top-level qualities. Within Reliability, recovery is ranked first among two children. What combined ROC weight does the recovery scenario receive if it is the only leaf below that child?
jeromy-evaluation.hint: Compute the two sibling weights separately, then multiply.
jeromy-evaluation.explanation: The rank-2-of-3 weight is (1/2 + 1/3)/3 = 5/18. Rank-1-of-2 is (1 + 1/2)/2 = 3/4. The path product is 5/18 × 3/4 × 1 = 5/24.
criteria: Uses 5/18 for the top-level weight
Uses 3/4 within the branch
Multiplies all weights along the path

jeromy-evaluation.title: A recommendation that changes
jeromy-evaluation.question: A decision has three scenario leaves ranked Recovery, Latency, Integration. Use ROC weights for this flat tree. Candidate C has ratings [3,1,0]; D has [1,2,3]. Compute the totals, then swap the priorities of Recovery and Latency while keeping each candidate’s ratings attached to the same scenarios. Which candidate leads in each case?
jeromy-evaluation.hint: For three siblings use 11/18, 5/18, 2/18. Reassign weights, not evidence, when priorities change.
jeromy-evaluation.answer: Initially C = 38/18 ≈ 2.1111 and D = 27/18 = 1.5000. After swapping priorities, C = 26/18 ≈ 1.4444 and D = 33/18 ≈ 1.8333. C leads first; D leads after the swap.
jeromy-evaluation.explanation: This is sensitivity to stakeholder priorities. The ratings have not changed. A sound recommendation states the priority assumptions and records why the stakeholder ordering is justified.
criteria: Correct ROC weights and totals
Reassigns weights without moving ratings to different scenarios
Explains the changed recommendation

jeromy-evaluation.title: Debt is not a fixed time balance
jeromy-evaluation.question: A team saves five weeks by omitting plugin support. Today the current design scores 0 and the desired design scores 3 on “add a new source”; its combined weight is 0.20. Other scenario ratings are equal. What is the weighted quality gap? Does this establish five weeks of repayment effort? What changes if the feature is no longer needed?
jeromy-evaluation.hint: Separate the delivery benefit, the quality gap, and the current effort estimate.
jeromy-evaluation.answer: The weighted gap is 0.20 × (3 − 0) = 0.60 on this scoring scale. It does not establish repayment effort. Estimate implementation and migration work now. If the feature loses business value, revisit the scenario and priorities; this particular gap may no longer justify investment.
jeromy-evaluation.explanation: Technical debt concerns a quality shortfall in context. A score is not measured in weeks, and desired quality can change.
criteria: Computes 0.60
Does not equate time saved with repayment effort
Reassesses current business value and quality targets

jeromy-resilience.title: Replicas with one shared trigger
jeromy-resilience.question: A service has six replicas across three regions, but the same automation can change the networking configuration of every replica at once. Which statement best describes the remaining risk?
jeromy-resilience.hint: Ask whether failure causes are independent.
jeromy-resilience.answer: A shared control mechanism can create correlated failure across otherwise separate replicas.
jeromy-resilience.explanation: Location diversity helps against some failures, but a global control action can cross those boundaries. Staged changes, isolation and independent recovery paths address different risks.
criteria: Distinguishes replica count from failure independence
Identifies the shared control plane
options: Six replicas guarantee availability
Three regions eliminate configuration risk
A shared control mechanism can fail all replicas together
Replication removes the need to test restoration

jeromy-resilience.title: Restore capacity or restore service?
jeromy-resilience.question: A recovered service handles 160 jobs/s. New work arrives at 130 jobs/s, and 9,000 durable jobs are waiting. Under a deterministic fluid model with no retries or other bottleneck, estimate the drain time. What if recovered capacity is only 120 jobs/s?
jeromy-resilience.hint: Only capacity left after new arrivals can drain the backlog.
jeromy-resilience.answer: At 160 jobs/s, spare capacity is 30 jobs/s; 9,000/30 = 300 seconds. At 120 jobs/s, the backlog grows by 10 jobs/s, so it cannot drain under these assumptions.
jeromy-resilience.explanation: Durability preserves work but does not guarantee timely recovery. Real estimates also need retry behavior, service-time variation, downstream limits and an explicit priority policy.
criteria: Computes spare capacity rather than total capacity
Obtains 300 seconds
Identifies instability at capacity 120 and states assumptions

jeromy-resilience.title: Design for diagnosing the outage
jeromy-resilience.question: A monitoring service uses its own ingestion pipeline to report all health signals. During an ingestion outage, operators lose dashboards. Propose two independent diagnostic or recovery mechanisms, and explain how to prioritize urgent alerts versus historical backfill.
jeromy-resilience.hint: Separate observing the failure from the component that has failed, and connect work priorities to customer impact.
jeromy-resilience.answer: Possible mechanisms include external synthetic probes with an independent alert path, and a separately reachable status/control service with retained diagnostic logs. Reserve capacity for urgent live signals and throttle historical backfill according to explicit data-loss and freshness requirements. Test the recovery path during a simulated ingestion failure.
jeromy-resilience.explanation: Independence is a property of dependencies, not just a different dashboard name. A backfill policy should state what is delayed or discarded and why.
criteria: Identifies independent dependencies
Connects prioritization to customer consequences
Includes a failure test and visibility during recovery

lizhi-performance.title: Local evidence is not the whole system
lizhi-performance.question: A repeatedly measured unit-level operation becomes 20% slower after a patch. What is the most defensible next step?
lizhi-performance.hint: Consider whether the operation is on a frequent path or a contended resource.
lizhi-performance.answer: Map the changed demand into a validated system model and assess representative workloads, then check predictions against system measurements.
lizhi-performance.explanation: A local change can be amplified near saturation, hidden off the critical path, or offset elsewhere. Functional success and a local slowdown alone do not determine end-to-end impact.
criteria: Separates local and system effects
Requires workload and validation evidence
options: Report exactly 20% worse system response
Ignore the change because functional tests pass
Map demand into a validated model and check representative system measurements
Treat one timing run as proof of a regression

lizhi-performance.title: Queueing amplifies a small change
lizhi-performance.question: In a single-server M/M/1 teaching model, arrival rate is 80 requests/s. Mean service demand changes from 8 ms to 10 ms. Calculate utilization and mean response time before and after. State why this is not a forecast for every production workload.
lizhi-performance.hint: Use ρ = λS with S in seconds, then R = S/(1−ρ); both utilizations must be below one.
lizhi-performance.answer: Before: ρ = 0.64 and R = 0.008/0.36 ≈ 22.22 ms. After: ρ = 0.80 and R = 0.010/0.20 = 50 ms. Service demand rises 25%, but predicted response rises 125%.
lizhi-performance.explanation: The nonlinear queueing effect depends on the stated Poisson arrivals, exponential independent service, single server, unbounded queue and steady-state assumptions. A real multi-resource system needs an appropriate model and validation.
criteria: Uses consistent units
Obtains 0.64, 0.80, 22.22 ms and 50 ms
Distinguishes service change from response change and states limits

lizhi-performance.title: Build a credible regression study
lizhi-performance.question: A teammate runs one baseline test and one updated test on different machines, then changes every service demand in a simulation until its output matches the update. Redesign this study so its conclusion is reviewable.
lizhi-performance.hint: Separate measurement control, model calibration and independent validation.
lizhi-performance.answer: Use comparable controlled environments and workloads, repeat measurements, and report distributions with statistical and practical effect evidence. Map affected code to modeled activities and update only justified parameters. Calibrate with baseline evidence, reserve independent measurements or workloads for validation, and report prediction error, variability and model limitations.
lizhi-performance.explanation: Fitting the model to the same result later called a validation target can conceal a poor causal model. Statistical significance alone is not a measure of user impact.
criteria: Controls environment and repeats runs
Maps local evidence to justified parameter changes
Uses independent validation and reports uncertainty
